hops.title: Alaska's 138-pound cabbage
hops.text: In 2012, Scott Robb of Palmer, Alaska, brought a 138.25-pound (63-kilogram) green cabbage to the Alaska State Fair, still the world record. Palmer, at 61.6° N, has a short, cool summer, but on the June solstice the Sun is up for 19 hours and 33 minutes and the sky never gets fully dark. Giant-variety genetics matter most, University of Alaska Fairbanks specialists note, but the long days play a big role. That is the table's 60° N row at work: around midsummer, long days beat the slant. The extension guide even describes a board platform that holds the cabbage as it grows and doubles as a stretcher at harvest.

hops.afterHeading: Oceans and mountains bend the pattern
hops.title: Bath toys that timed a loop of North Pacific currents
hops.text: In January 1992, a North Pacific storm washed a container of 29,000 plastic bath toys (ducks, turtles, frogs and beavers) off a ship bound from Hong Kong to Tacoma, Washington. Ten months later they started landing near Sitka, Alaska. Sitka collector Dean Orbison kept about a hundred of them in a cabinet of curiosities and logged each year's finds from 1994 to 2004. When oceanographer Curtis Ebbesmeyer graphed that logbook over coffee, four peaks appeared, roughly three years apart. The peaks helped him estimate that floating things take about three years to ride wind-driven, Coriolis-turned currents around the North Pacific Subpolar Gyre, a counterclockwise loop thousands of miles around.

hops.title: Fairbanks and Tucson get about the same yearly precipitation
hops.text: A desert sounds like any place with very little yearly rain. Yet in NOAA's 1991 to 2020 normals, Fairbanks, Alaska, gets 296 mm of precipitation a year and Tucson, Arizona, gets 270 mm, about an inch apart. Fairbanks sits in boreal spruce forest; Tucson is surrounded by the saguaros of the Sonoran Desert. July shows how warmth changes the reading. July rain is almost the same: 57 mm in Fairbanks, 56 mm in Tucson. At 17 °C, Fairbanks's dry line is 34 mm; at 31 °C, Tucson's is 62 mm. On a Walter-Lieth diagram, the same rain makes a humid July in Fairbanks and a dry one in Tucson.

audio.title: A two-minute thaw, a penguin on the equator, and waist-high pines
audio.transcript:
Climate rules look tidy on a globe. Here are three true places where air, water and soil bent them.

First, Spearfish, South Dakota, on the morning of January twenty-second, nineteen forty-three. The town sat in a shallow pool of Arctic air at the foot of the Black Hills, at four below zero Fahrenheit, about minus twenty Celsius. Warmer Pacific air lay just above that cold pool. At seven thirty-two, the cold layer drew back like an ebbing tide, a comparison made by the Weather Bureau meteorologist who wrote the day up, and the warm air reached the town. In two minutes the thermometer jumped forty-nine degrees Fahrenheit, about twenty-seven Celsius, to forty-five above zero. After some wild swings it reached fifty-four by nine o'clock. Then the cold pool sloshed back, and in twenty-seven minutes Spearfish fell fifty-eight degrees, right back to four below. Across the region that day, plate-glass windows cracked in the town of Lead, and in Rapid City motorists had to park until they could clear a thick frost that formed almost instantly on their windshields.

Second, a penguin on the equator. If latitude wrote all the rules, the equator is the last place you would look for one. Yet the Galápagos penguin, about half a metre tall, nests in caves and holes in the volcanic rock of Fernandina and Isabela islands and hunts small fish such as sardines. It is the only penguin that lives on the equator, and the northern tip of Isabela puts some of them just north of it. Moving water makes this possible. The Humboldt Current carries cool water north along South America, and the deep Cromwell Current wells up against the islands where the penguins live, chilling the sea and bringing up nutrients. That gift has a catch. During a strong El Niño, the cold upwelling weakens, the sea warms, the penguins struggle to find enough fish, and their numbers can crash. In the El Niño of nineteen eighty-two and eighty-three, they fell by more than three quarters.

Third, a hillside on the Mendocino coast of California. Here the land rises in a staircase of old sea floors: five wave-cut terraces, lifted out of the ocean by the moving plates, each step about a hundred thousand years older than the one below. At Jug Handle State Natural Reserve, a nature trail passes coast redwoods and grand firs and reaches pygmy forest on the third step. The nearby Hans Jenny Pygmy Forest Reserve sits on the oldest step, more than half a million years old. Over all that time, rain has leached nutrients from the upper soil, leaving it acidic and poor, above a hard layer that roots and water struggle to cross. On the poorest soils, some mature Mendocino cypresses and Bolander pines are only about two and a half feet tall. That reserve gets about thirty-nine inches of rain a year, in a mild, foggy coastal climate. Climate made the first guess, a forest. The soil decided how tall it could grow.
